title: Illness as expiation
hookLine: no tiredness, illness or worry touches a believer, not even a thorn's prick, without wiping away some sins

lines: THE SMALLEST THING ON THE LIST.
cards: A thorn. Small enough to pull out with your fingernails, sharp enough to make you say ow. It's in a hadith, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it's the smallest thing on a list.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, names what can happen to a believer: tiredness, illness, worry, sorrow, harm, distress. And then he goes all the way down, to the prick of a thorn.
Even that, he says, is not for nothing. Today is about why.

teach.h: EVEN THE PRICK OF A THORN.
teach.b: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. No tiredness, no illness, no worry, no sorrow, no harm and no distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, without Allah wiping away some of his sins by it.
The word for that is kaffarah, expiation. In this picture, the hard hours of being sick are not empty hours. Something is happening in them, even when the person lying there can do nothing at all.
Al-Bukhari keeps a story that shows how this was lived.

Ibn 'Abbas once pointed out a woman to a student and said: shall I show you a woman of the people of Paradise? She had come to the Prophet with an illness that made her fall in fits, and asked him to pray for her cure.
He gave her a choice. If you wish, be patient, and you will have Paradise. Or if you wish, I will pray to Allah to heal you.
She chose patience. But she asked for one thing: that when the fits came, she wouldn't be uncovered. And he prayed for that.
Now the other side, so the picture isn't bent. Patience here doesn't mean refusing a doctor.
A hadith in Abu Dawud says, in paraphrase, that Allah sent down both disease and its remedy, so seek treatment. The medicine and the patience aren't rivals. You take the pills.
You wait for the results. And the waiting, in this hadith, counts too.

how: Muslims who are ill often recall the hadith that illness and even a thorn's prick wipe away sins, and pair patience with seeking medical treatment, which the hadith also encourage.

o: hardships, even a thorn's prick, wiping away some of one's sins
a gift brought to someone sick when you visit them
a fast kept to make up for the days missed while you were sick

games.q: illness as expiation — tap the pairs.
p: the smallest thing on the list

s: in the hadith, only serious illness wipes away sins
the list goes all the way down to the prick of a thorn.
in the story, the woman asked not to be uncovered during her fits
she chose patience, and the Prophet prayed for that.
patience in illness means refusing medicine
a hadith in Abu Dawud says Allah sent the remedy too, so seek treatment.

games.q: you're ill, and the Prophet offers you a choice: be patient and have Paradise, or he'll pray for your cure. what do you choose?
o: patience, but ask not to be uncovered.
games.why: in al-Bukhari, the woman chose patience and asked only not to be uncovered during her fits, and he prayed for that.

practice: Scan your body slowly, head to feet, and find something tired, aching, or not quite right: a stiff neck, a tired back, a worry sitting in your chest. Don't fight it; let your attention rest on it, and breathe around it.
If nothing hurts today, think of someone for whom something does, and if you pray, hold that ache up as it is.

wordCard.voice: Illness as expiation. In the hadith, even a thorn's prick wipes away some sins; the hard hours are not empty. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: expiation, the wiping away of sins.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing is wasted. The pills, the waiting and the patience all count. Glad you're here.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5641–5642 (no tiredness, illness, worry … not even a thorn's prick, but Allah expiates sins by it)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5652 (Ibn 'Abbas: the woman with fits who chose patience)
Sunan Abi Dawud 3874 (Allah sent down the disease and the remedy; seek treatment)
